Konstantin Tsiolkovsky. Russian schoolteacher and visionary who developed the mathematical rocket equation and conceived the entire architecture of space exploration. Though he never built a working rocket, Tsiolkovsky's theoretical work, published in obscure journals and largely unknown to the West during his lifetime, became the foundation of Soviet cosmonautics and is now recognized as the starting point of modern astronautics.

He derived the Tsiolkovsky equation, which relates a rocket's delta-v, or change in velocity, to its mass ratio and exhaust velocity. This is the fundamental law governing all rocket motion. Tsiolkovsky designed the multi-stage rocket concept and argued that only a staged vehicle could escape Earth's gravity and reach orbit. He proposed using liquid propellants, particularly liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, for efficiency — this was decades before anyone built such engines.

Beyond rockets, he conceived of space stations, long-duration spaceflight, and artificial gravity via rotation. These were science fiction concepts he grounded in physics. Tsiolkovsky worked in near-total isolation in Kaluga, a provincial Russian city, publishing in obscure Russian journals that few Western scientists read until after World War II.

After the nineteen-seventeen Russian Revolution, he became a celebrated figure in the Soviet state and collaborated with rocket societies. His legacy became the philosophical core of Soviet space ambition, directly inspiring Sergei Korolev and the designers who would make Tsiolkovsky's vision of orbit a reality.
